primitives.name: Constrained Batch Objective
primitives.verbatim_quote: Equations & assumptions - Constrained batch objective: argmax_{x1:n⊆D_pool} a({x1,...,xn}, p(ω|D_train)) s.t.
primitives.latex: \arg\max_{x_{1:n} \subseteq D_{\text{pool}}} a(\{x_1, \ldots, x_n\}, p(\omega | D_{\text{train}})) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad c(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \leq c_{\text{max}}, \; n \leq n_{\text{max}}
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'x_{1:n}': 'samples in batch, dimensionless', 'D_{\\text{pool}}': 'pool of unlabeled samples, dimensionless', 'a': 'acquisition function value, bits', 'p(\\omega | D_{\\text{train}})': 'posterior distribution over weights, dimensionless', 'c(x)': 'cost of sample x, dollars', 'c_{\\text{max}}': 'maximum batch cost, dollars', 'n_{\\text{max}}': 'maximum batch size, samples'}
primitives.assumptions: Per-sample costs known before selection; order-dependent costs allowed; pool-based sampling; MC-dropout provides valid epistemic uncertainty.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When c(x) exceeds remaining budget, batch selection fails due to infeasibility.

layer2.mapping: The constrained optimization mirrors GSI's Bayesian update under information-theoretic constraints, where acquisition functions guide posterior refinement.
layer2.telemetry: Number of AL iterations required to reach target accuracy under budget.

primitives.name: Batch BALD Mutual Information
primitives.verbatim_quote: - Batch-BALD acquisition: a_BatchBALD = I(y1:n; ω | x1:n, D_train) = H(y1:n|x1:n,D_train) - E_{p(ω|D_train)}[H(y1:n|x1:n,ω,D_train)] (Eq.
primitives.latex: a_{\text{BatchBALD}} = I(y_{1:n}; \omega | x_{1:n}, D_{\text{train}}) = H(y_{1:n}|x_{1:n}, D_{\text{train}}) - \mathbb{E}_{p(\omega|D_{\text{train}})}[H(y_{1:n}|x_{1:n}, \omega, D_{\text{train}})]
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'y_{1:n}': 'labels for batch, dimensionless', 'ω': 'model weights, dimensionless', 'x_{1:n}': 'input features for batch, dimensionless', 'D_{\\text{train}}': 'training dataset, dimensionless', 'I': 'mutual information, bits', 'H': 'entropy, bits'}
primitives.assumptions: MC-dropout approximates true posterior; joint predictive entropy captures model uncertainty.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Infinite-budget limit reduces to standard Batch-BALD without constraints.

layer2.mapping: Batch-BALD serves as a kernel for GSI's probabilistic inference engine, quantifying label informativeness through entropy differences.
layer2.telemetry: Expected reduction in label entropy post-acquisition.

primitives.name: Dynamic Thresholding
primitives.verbatim_quote: - Dynamic threshold: c_th,i = c_max,i/(n_max - (i-1)), c_max,i = c_max,i-1 - c(x*_{i-1}).
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'c_{\\text{th},i}': 'threshold cost at step i, dollars', 'c_{\\text{max},i}': 'remaining budget at step i, dollars', 'x^*_{i-1}': 'selected sample at previous step, dimensionless', 'i': 'iteration index, dimensionless'}
primitives.assumptions: Budget shrinks after each selection; threshold adjusts adaptively based on remaining capacity.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Expensive but highly informative samples may be excluded if they exceed current threshold.

layer2.mapping: Dynamic thresholding aligns with GSE’s weekly charting budgeting logic, where cost thresholds evolve with available slots.
layer2.telemetry: Proportion of high-value samples rejected due to thresholding.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core innovation lies in extending Batch-BALD to constrained settings by introducing two heuristics: dynamic thresholding and greedy knapsack. The former ensures feasible selections within shrinking budgets, while the latter prioritizes costly yet informative samples. These primitives form a dual framework for balancing exploration and exploitation under budgetary constraints. In the infinite-budget limit, both strategies converge to standard Batch-BALD, indicating robustness. However, the NP-hard nature of the knapsack problem introduces heuristic approximations that break submodularity, leading to potential inefficiencies. This duality reflects a fundamental tension between computational tractability and optimality in active learning. The geospatial cost models used in the original paper are replaced in GSE with dollar-cost equivalents, enabling deployment in analyst scheduling contexts. The dynamic thresholding mechanism is particularly sensitive to early selections, which can starve out expensive but valuable samples—a failure mode critical to avoid in GSE’s charting workflows.
